opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's the missing piece. If you look at current AI systems, LLMs in particular, they're very good at manipulating language, but they don't really understand the physical world. They can't plan, they don't have persistent memory, and they can't really reason in the sense of searching for a sequence of actions that will achieve a goal. A house cat has a better model of the physical world than the biggest LLM we have.

So what's an action-conditioned world model? It's a system that, given an estimate of the current state of the world and an action you might take, predicts the resulting state. Once you have that, you can do planning. You can imagine a sequence of actions, use your world model to predict the outcome, and optimize that sequence to satisfy some objective while respecting some guardrails. That's what humans and animals do all the time. It's what psychologists call System 2, and current LLMs basically don't have it. They produce one token after another, reactively.

The key is that you can't build these by predicting every pixel. The world is too unpredictable at that level of detail. That's why generative models for video haven't really worked for this purpose. You need to make predictions in an abstract representation space, which is the idea behind joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA. You learn a representation that throws away the details you can't predict, and you predict in that space.

Why near-term? Because we're starting to see it work. We've had results with V-JEPA and follow-ups where you pre-train on lots of video, then fine-tune with a relatively small amount of interaction data, and you get a robot arm that can plan zero-shot to accomplish tasks in environments it has never seen. No reinforcement learning with millions of trials, no task-specific training. That's a big deal.

And the applications are obvious: robotics first, of course. Everybody's building humanoid robots right now, and the dirty secret of that industry is that nobody knows how to make them smart enough to be generally useful. World models are how you get there. But it goes beyond robotics: any system that needs to predict the consequences of its actions, whether that's in industrial control, autonomous driving, or even agentic systems acting in software environments.

So my prediction is that within the next few years, this architecture is going to become the dominant paradigm, and people will look back and say, "Why were we trying to get to human-level intelligence just by scaling up autoregressive LLMs?" It's not going to happen that way. You need systems that understand the world, and that's what world models give you.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the short answer is that it's the piece we're missing. If you look at what large language models can do, they're very good at manipulating language, because language is discrete, it's low-bandwidth, and there's a lot of it lying around. But language is a very poor approximation of how the world actually works. A ten-year-old can clear the dinner table and load the dishwasher. A cat can plan a sequence of jumps to get onto the top of the refrigerator. We don't have robots that can do either of those things reliably, and it's not because we lack the motors. It's because the systems don't have a model of what happens when they act.

So an action-conditioned world model is very simple to state. You have a representation of the state of the world at time t, you have an action you're considering, and the model predicts the representation of the state at time t plus one. Once you have that, you can do planning. You can imagine a sequence of actions, roll it forward in your head, and pick the sequence that gets you to the goal you want, or that minimizes some cost. That's what humans and animals do all the time. That's what we mean by common sense, really, this ability to predict the consequences of actions without having to try everything.

Why do I say near-term? Because the ingredients are starting to come together. We now know how to learn good representations from video in a self-supervised way, with things like JEPA, the joint embedding predictive architecture, where instead of predicting every pixel, which is hopeless because the world is not fully predictable, you predict in an abstract representation space and let the model discard the details it can't predict. Once you have that representation, conditioning the prediction on an action is a fairly natural extension. And the applications are immediate: robotics, obviously, but also planning in any domain where you have a simulator or sensors, manufacturing, logistics, autonomous driving, scientific experiments.

The other reason I think it's near-term is economic. Every company that builds physical systems has a mountain of sensor data and video that nobody has figured out how to use for anything except monitoring. If you can learn a world model from that data, you unlock planning and control, and that's worth a great deal more than a chatbot that writes your emails.

Now, I want to be careful. I don't think we're going to have human-level world models next year. The hard part is learning hierarchical representations so you can plan at multiple time scales, at the level of "go to the kitchen" and also at the level of individual joint torques. We don't have that yet. But the first-order version, a single-level world model that lets a robot plan a few seconds ahead, that's within reach, and I think it will have a lot of impact before the more ambitious stuff arrives.

astra-6.text:
Well, the idea is to train a system to predict what will happen in the world as a consequence of an action. If I move this object, or if a robot turns left, what happens next? If you have a model that can answer that, you can use it to plan: imagine a sequence of actions, predict the outcome, and select actions that get you closer to your objective.

The important thing is that you don’t necessarily have to predict every detail. If you’re driving, you don’t need to predict the exact appearance of every leaf on every tree. You need to predict the things that matter for your decisions—the motion of other vehicles, where the road goes, whether an obstacle is in your path. So we want predictions in an abstract representation space, rather than necessarily generating every pixel.

That’s promising because there is an enormous amount of structure in the world that systems can learn from observation. Then, with action-conditioned learning, they can learn how their own actions affect it. You don’t have to discover everything by physically trying every possible action, which can be expensive or dangerous.

I think the near-term opportunities are in relatively constrained settings, where you can learn a useful model and use it for control or planning. You don’t need to solve all of intelligence before that becomes useful.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if you want an AI system to help you do things, it needs to predict the consequences of actions. A language model can tell you what sounds like a reasonable sequence of steps, but that’s different from having a model of how the world will change when you act.

An action-conditioned world model takes the current situation and a possible action, and predicts what happens next. Then you can use that model to plan: consider several sequences of actions, predict their outcomes, and select one that satisfies your objective.

You don’t necessarily have to predict every detail. If you’re moving a glass across a table, you care about where the glass ends up and whether it falls over. You don’t need to predict the exact texture of every pixel. So the challenge is to learn representations that capture the aspects of the world that matter for prediction and control.

That’s promising because you can start with limited environments, where the actions and objectives are well defined. You don’t have to solve all of intelligence at once to build something useful.
